Discomfort as a Methodological Condition: When Reflexivity Is Not Enough in Ethnography
abstract: Reflexivity has become a central ethical and methodological imperative in contemporary ethnography, routinely framed as a means through which researchers manage discomfort, resolve ethical tension, and maintain accountability in the field. Yet reflexivity does not always dissolve discomfort, but it can intensify it. Drawing on ethnographic fieldwork with religious minorities in Pakistan, shaped by asymmetrical power, uneven trust, and unsettled obligation, this article argues that discomfort is not a failure of method to be corrected but a methodological condition through which ethnographic knowledge is produced. Through a series of fieldwork vignettes, I demonstrate how moments of ethical unease when empathy proves insufficient, reciprocity impossible, and responsibility unresolved generate critical insight rather than methodological breakdown. I identify four functions discomfort performs: signalling structural asymmetry, limit-testing ethical frameworks, registering relational excess, and enabling epistemological reorientation. By reconceptualizing discomfort as constitutive rather than incidental to ethnographic practice, this article challenges normative expectations of reflexive resolution and contributes to ongoing debates on ethics, positionality, and method in qualitative research.

title: When interactive advantage reverses: AI, authenticity erosion and dynamic multi-channel performance
journal: Journal of Research in Interactive Marketing
abstract: Purpose Brands today face a striking managerial anomaly: artificial intelligence (AI)-driven content volume has surged by over 35% year-on-year, yet engagement rates have stagnated or declined. This study asks why early interactive performance gains so reliably reverse and identifies two novel findings that resolve this puzzle. First, authenticity erosion does not merely accompany relationship quality decline; it precedes and amplifies it, serving as the earliest detectable warning of relational reversal. Second, a higher AI-content share compresses the temporal window between initial performance gains and their reversal, accelerating the curvature of the interactive advantage trajectory. Design/methodology/approach A two-study, multi-method design integrates a natural language processing (NLP)-driven event-study difference-in-differences (Study 1) to trace temporal escalation effects on relational tone, authenticity and performance, with dynamic system generalized method of moments (GMM) panel modelling (Study 2) to uncover lagged mechanisms involving interactive intensity, AI-content share, relationship quality and authenticity. Findings Interactive escalation follows a non-monotonic inverted-U trajectory: initial gains give way to relational reversal as authenticity erodes, parasocial bonds weaken and relationship quality declines. Authenticity erosion is the leading signal of this reversal, preceding broader relational decline. Higher AI-content share compresses the gain-to-decline window, steepening and advancing the curvature through a negative interaction between AI share, interactive intensity and perceived authenticity. Originality/value Unlike prior static models assuming linear/diminishing returns or classical wear-out, this research formalises “reversible advantage” as a path-dependent process, with AI accelerating curvature. It bridges theory-practice gaps by offering diagnostic pacing heuristics, advancing interactive marketing with empirical evidence on temporal advantage cycles in AI ecosystems.

title: What you have makes you healthy: the effect of digital skills on the mental health of rural migrant workers
abstract: Purpose In the increasingly developing digital economy, it is easier for rural migrant workers with digital skills to obtain job advantages and social support, which can potentially affect their mental health. However, few studies have explored the impact of digital skills on the mental health of rural migrant workers. The purpose of this article is to examine the impact of digital skills and the channels through which this impact occurs. Design/methodology/approach This article extends Grossman's health demand model to theoretically analyze the impact of digital skills on the mental health of rural migrant workers. It then empirically tests this relationship using data from the China Family Panel Studies in 2018, 2020 and 2022, employing fixed-effects models, instrumental variable methods, as well as mediation and moderation effect models. Findings The IV estimation indicates that an increase in the digital skills index by one unit reduces the average depression score of rural migrant workers by 2.372 points. Therefore, the improvement of digital skills is associated with lower depression scores and better mental health. Second, the impact varies by skill level, migration scope and the type of digital skills involved. The digital skills of low-skilled and rural migrant workers flowing within the province have significant impact on their mental health, while the digital skills of high-skilled and rural migrant workers flowing between the province have no significant. Digital workplace and social skills significantly affect RMWs' mental health, whereas other digital skills show a statistically insignificant association. Third, wage level, health behavior, utilization of medical services and job satisfaction are the channels by which digital skills are associated with the mental health of rural migrant workers. Finally, working conditions, schedules and exposure to certain risks moderate the impact of digital skills on rural migrant workers' mental health. As working conditions improve, work schedules become more flexible and the work environment becomes safer, the positive effect of digital skills on rural migrant workers' mental health becomes more pronounced. Originality/value First, this article extends Grossman's health demand model to theoretically analyze the impact of digital skills on rural migrant workers' mental health and its channels, while providing empirical evidence for such causal effects. This contributes to the literature on how human capital influences migrant workers' health outcomes. Second, we identify significant heterogeneity in these effects across skill levels, migration patterns and types of digital skills. Third, the results reveal four key mediating pathways: wage level, health behavior, utilization of medical services and job satisfaction. Finally, working conditions, schedules and exposure to certain risks are found to play moderating roles in this relationship.

title: Understanding decarbonization barriers interactions in the Portuguese port system
journal: The International Journal of Logistics Management
abstract: Purpose Ports, as critical nodes in maritime logistics and supply chains, face growing pressure to decarbonize, yet progress remains slow. While existing research identifies multiple barriers to port decarbonization, limited attention has been paid to how these barriers interact and mutually reinforce one another. This study aims to identify key barriers to port decarbonization and to analyze their interrelationships to uncover the root causes of decarbonization challenges. Design/methodology/approach Adopting a sociotechnical systems (STS) perspective, the study combines interpretive structural modeling (ISM) and the matrix of cross-impact multiplications applied to classification (MICMAC) approach. Seventeen decarbonization barriers were identified through a literature review and semi-structured interviews with experts from the Portuguese port system. ISM was used to develop a hierarchical model of barrier interactions, while MICMAC classified barriers according to their driving and dependence power. Findings The findings reveal that barriers to port decarbonization form a highly interconnected system. External environment barriers, which are external challenges coming from outside the ports' organizational boundaries, emerged as dominant root drivers. Examples include global policy gaps and instability, lack of government support and industry complexity. Intermediate challenges related to standards, data availability, funding and knowledge. Those issues function as critical transmission mechanisms between root barriers and highly visible ones. Frequently cited challenges, such as high costs and technological immaturity, appear largely as dependent outcomes rather than primary causes. Originality/value This study advances port decarbonization research by moving beyond barrier prioritization toward a multi-level explanation of barrier interactions. By integrating STS theory with ISM-MICMAC analysis, it provides novel insights into where effective intervention points lie in port decarbonization efforts.

title: The thrift bridge
abstract: Purpose This paper aims to review the latest management developments across the globe and pinpoint practical implications from cutting-edge research and case studies. Design/methodology/approach This briefing is prepared by an independent writer who adds their own impartial comments and places the articles in context. Findings Frugality is the practical mechanism that converts abstract sustainability values into actual responsible consumption, making thrifty, reuse-and-repair-minded consumers a high-converting segment for businesses—provided the responsible option isn’t framed as a costly luxury. Originality/value The briefing saves busy executives, strategists and researchers hours of reading time by selecting only the very best, most pertinent information and presenting it in a condensed and easy-to-digest format.

Talent management practices and employee career sustainability: the role of employee career adaptability and psychological well-being
journal: European Journal of Training and Development
abstract: Purpose Maintaining a meaningful and advancing career is a significant challenge in the hospitality industry due to customer-facing pressures, job instability and limited advancement opportunities. This study aims to examine how talent management practices (TMPs) enhance employee career sustainability, focusing on the mediating roles of career adaptability and psychological well-being and the moderating role of inclusive leadership. Design/methodology/approach A time-lagged survey design was used to collect data from hospitality employees (i.e. hotel staff) in China. A serial moderated mediation analysis was performed using Mplus to evaluate the proposed model. Findings The results support the proposed model, indicating that TMPs significantly enhance career sustainability both directly and indirectly through career adaptability and psychological well-being. Moreover, inclusive leadership strengthens the proposed relationship by creating a supportive and empowering work environment. Originality/value This research enhances the understanding of career sustainability by introducing a new antecedent (e.g. TMPs), a dual mediation model, and by identifying inclusive leadership as a boundary condition. It contributes to the hospitality literature by integrating career construction and social exchange theories within the framework of hospitality management.

title: Exploring the Interconnected Drivers of Sustainable Employee and Organisational Performance: Insights From Senior Management in the KwaZulu-Natal Education Sector, South Africa
journal: International Journal of Sustainability in Business and Economics
abstract: Sustainable employee and organisational performance in the public education sector is shaped by an interdependent system of leadership competence, human resource practices, organisational culture, skills development, knowledge sharing, communication structures, and contextual resource constraints. These drivers are particularly salient at Senior Management Service (SMS) level, where strategic leadership, policy implementation, accountability, and institutional governance converge. This qualitative study explored the interconnected drivers of sustainable performance through the lived experiences of senior managers within the KwaZulu-Natal Department of Education. Using semi-structured interviews, the study captured nuanced insights into the enablers and barriers influencing the implementation and functionality of the Performance Management and Development System (PMDS). Thematic analysis revealed that while PMDS is intended to enhance accountability and continuous improvement, its sustainability is undermined by limited leadership commitment, inadequate developmental support, fragmented internal communication, skills mismatches, weak knowledge-sharing mechanisms, entrenched compliance-driven organisational cultures, and persistent financial and human resource constraints. These interrelated challenges constrain both individual capability and organisational capacity, weakening the translation of employee performance into sustainable organisational outcomes. In addressing the study’s objectives, the findings support an integrated, systems-oriented approach to performance management that prioritises visible and sustained leadership engagement, competency-based and continuous capacity development, learning-oriented organisational cultures, digitally enabled performance and knowledge management systems, and strategic resource alignment. Addressing these drivers holistically is essential for fostering sustainable employee and organisational performance and contributes to ongoing debates on strengthening performance management and human resource sustainability in public sector institutions within developing country contexts.
